steps.eyebrow: Customizing plot appearance with rcParams and styles
steps.title: Style sheets, rcParams, and seaborn palettes
steps.lede: matplotlib's default look is functional. Three tools let you change it.

blocks.text: plt.style.use('style-name') applies one of matplotlib's predefined style sheets—for example 'ggplot' or 'dark_background'. The available styles can be listed with plt.style.available. Calling it once changes the look of every plot drawn after that call.

For finer control, rcParams can be set directly. After import matplotlib as mpl, mpl.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2 sets the default line width for every plot drawn after that call. A custom style file can set properties such as 'axes.titlesize', 'lines.linewidth', or tick label sizes.

sns.set_palette('pastel') sets the matplotlib color cycle from a seaborn palette, applying that color scheme to subsequent plots. This is separate from sns.set_theme() and affects only the color sequence.

before.code:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
# Default matplotlib style
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [21, 23, 19, 25, 20])
ax.set_title('Delivery Times')
plt.show()

annotations.text: Default: blue line, white background, no grid

after.code:
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
plt.style.use('ggplot')
mpl.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [21, 23, 19, 25, 20])
ax.set_title('Delivery Times')
plt.show()

annotations.text: plt.style.use applies a predefined style sheet
rcParams sets a specific default globally

blocks.change_summary: plt.style.use() and rcParams change the overall look; sns.set_palette() changes the color cycle.

public.prompt: Which call applies matplotlib's built-in `'ggplot'` style sheet to all subsequent plots?

opt_correct.message: Correct. `plt.style.use('ggplot')` applies one of matplotlib's predefined style sheets; the available styles can be listed with `plt.style.available`.

opt_sns.message: `sns.set_theme()` applies seaborn's built-in themes, not matplotlib style sheets. To apply a matplotlib style sheet like `'ggplot'`, use `plt.style.use()`.

opt_rcparams.message: `mpl.rcParams` sets individual style properties (like `'lines.linewidth'`), not a whole style sheet. To apply a named style sheet, use `plt.style.use('ggplot')`.

opt_apply.message: `plt.style.apply()` is not a valid function. The correct function is `plt.style.use('style-name')`.

correct.message: Right. `plt.style.use('style-name')` applies a predefined style sheet; you can see all available names with `plt.style.available`.

incorrect.message: `plt.style.use('style-name')` is the function that applies a matplotlib style sheet. Pass the style name as a string, for example `plt.style.use('ggplot')`.

hints: The function lives in the `plt.style` namespace and is called `use`.
Style names are strings — for example `'ggplot'` or `'dark_background'`.

public.prompt: A team wants all their plots to use a specific brand color palette from seaborn. Which call sets the matplotlib color cycle to that palette for all subsequent plots?

opt_set_palette.message: Correct. `sns.set_palette(palette, ...)` sets the matplotlib color cycle from a seaborn palette, applying that color scheme to subsequent plots.

opt_style_use.message: `plt.style.use()` applies a matplotlib style sheet by name. `'pastel'` is a seaborn palette name, not a matplotlib style sheet name — use `sns.set_palette('pastel')` instead.

correct.message: Correct. `sns.set_palette()` is the dedicated function for setting the matplotlib color cycle from a seaborn palette.

incorrect.message: `sns.set_palette('palette-name')` sets the matplotlib color cycle from a seaborn palette, applying that color scheme to all subsequent plots.

import matplotlib as mpl

steps.title: A grid of Axes in one Figure
steps.lede: plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) creates a Figure containing a grid of Axes.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to show the delivery-time histogram and the distance/delivery-time scatter plot together, side by side, instead of as two separate figures. fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) creates a Figure containing a grid of Axes with the given number of rows and columns. plt.subplots(2, 2) creates a 2×2 grid of four Axes inside one Figure.

Each Axes in the returned grid is indexed separately—for example axs[0, 0] for the top-left panel. Plotting and labeling calls made on one Axes only affect that panel. axs[0, 0].hist(data) draws a histogram into the top-left panel; axs[0, 1].scatter(x_values, y_values) draws a scatter into the top-right panel without disturbing the first.

blocks.alt_text: A 2×2 grid of empty Axes boxes inside a single Figure boundary. Each box is labelled with its index: axs[0,0] top-left, axs[0,1] top-right, axs[1,0] bottom-left, axs[1,1] bottom-right.

segments.label: Creating a subplot grid and plotting independently on each Axes
segments.summary: The instructor motivates splitting data across multiple panels rather than crowding one figure, then shows how the nrows and ncols arguments to plt.subplots control the shape of the returned Axes collection. Printing the result for a 1×1, 2×1, and 2×2 call reveals how the return value changes from a single Axes to a flat list to a nested list of lists. The instructor then simplifies to a 2×1 grid, unpacks the two Axes into separate variables, and assigns distinct plot calls, legends, titles, and axis labels to each — producing one figure with two fully independent panels.

blocks.group_title: Building a multi-panel figure: grid layout and independent axes

bridge.before: Watch how the nrows/ncols arguments change the shape of the returned collection, and how each panel receives its own plot call without affecting the other. Note: the clip unpacks axes into named variables (ax1, ax2) rather than using index notation like axs[0, 0]; both approaches are equivalent.
bridge.after: The key takeaway is that each Axes is independent — calls on one panel never touch another. The teaching text also covers 2×2 indexing (axs[0, 0]) which the clip omits.

public.prompt: After `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)`, you want to draw a histogram in the top-right panel only. Which call is correct?

options.text: `plt.hist(data)` — it automatically goes to the top-right panel

opt_correct.message: Correct. `axs[0, 1]` selects row 0 (top), column 1 (right). Calling `.hist()` on that Axes draws only into that panel.

opt_wrong_index.message: `axs[1, 0]` selects row 1 (bottom), column 0 (left) — that is the bottom-left panel, not the top-right. The top-right is `axs[0, 1]`.

opt_fig.message: The Figure object does not have a `hist()` method. Plotting calls go on individual Axes objects, indexed as `axs[row, col]`.

opt_plt.message: `plt.hist()` draws on the current active Axes, not necessarily the top-right panel. To target a specific panel, use `axs[0, 1].hist(data)`.

correct.message: Right. In a 2×2 grid, `axs[0, 1]` is row 0 (top), column 1 (right). Calls on that Axes only affect that panel.

incorrect.message: In a 2×2 grid, rows and columns are 0-indexed: `axs[0, 0]` is top-left, `axs[0, 1]` is top-right, `axs[1, 0]` is bottom-left, `axs[1, 1]` is bottom-right.

hints: The first index is the row (0 = top, 1 = bottom); the second is the column (0 = left, 1 = right).

public.prompt:
A DataFrame `df` with columns `col_a`, `col_b`, `col_c`, and `col_d` is already loaded.

Create a 2×2 subplot grid and draw a histogram in each panel:
1. Create a 2×2 grid using `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)`
2. Draw a histogram of `col_a` in the top-left panel: `axs[0, 0].hist(df['col_a'])`
3. Draw a histogram of `col_b` in the top-right panel: `axs[0, 1].hist(df['col_b'])`
4. Draw a histogram of `col_c` in the bottom-left panel: `axs[1, 0].hist(df['col_c'])`
5. Draw a histogram of `col_d` in the bottom-right panel: `axs[1, 1].hist(df['col_d'])`

Each panel will show the distribution of one column.

solution_files.content:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

# Data (already loaded)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    'col_a': [23, 25, 22, 24, 26, 23, 25, 24],
    'col_b': [45, 47, 44, 46, 48, 45, 47, 46],
    'col_c': [56, 58, 55, 57, 59, 56, 58, 57],
    'col_d': [78, 80, 77, 79, 81, 78, 80, 79]
})

# Create a 2x2 subplot grid and draw histograms below
fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)
axs[0, 0].hist(df['col_a'])
axs[0, 1].hist(df['col_b'])
axs[1, 0].hist(df['col_c'])
axs[1, 1].hist(df['col_d'])

correct.message: Excellent! You created a 2×2 subplot grid and drew a distinct histogram in each panel — each Axes is independent.

incorrect.message: Make sure you used `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)` to create the grid, then called `.hist()` on each of the four `axs[row, col]` objects with a different column.

hints: Start with `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2)` to get a 2×2 grid of Axes.
Each panel is addressed by `axs[row, col]` — for example `axs[0, 0]` is top-left and `axs[1, 1]` is bottom-right.

blocks.text: plt.style.use('style-name') applies a predefined style sheet. mpl.rcParams['lines.linewidth'] = 2 sets a specific default globally. sns.set_palette('pastel') sets the color cycle from a seaborn palette.
fig, axs = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols) creates a Figure with a grid of Axes. Each Axes is indexed separately (axs[0, 0]) and plotting calls on one panel don't affect the others.

blocks.text: When plt.subplots(2, 2) returns axs, think of it as a 2D grid. axs[0, 0] is the top-left panel, axs[0, 1] is top-right, axs[1, 0] is bottom-left, axs[1, 1] is bottom-right. Plotting on axs[0, 0] only affects that one panel—the others stay empty until you plot on them.
